+# ADR 0001: Raise Pricing Cache TTL from 900 to 3600 Seconds
+
+## Status
+
+Accepted
+
+## Context
+
+The pricing service currently caches responses with a time-to-live (TTL) of 900 seconds (15 minutes). This duration was chosen as a balance between freshness and cache efficiency, but operational experience has shown that pricing data changes infrequently in practice. Most pricing updates occur during scheduled maintenance windows or as part of deliberate business decisions, rather than continuously or in response to real-time market conditions. The frequent cache invalidation at 15-minute intervals creates unnecessary load on the pricing service backend and generates redundant cache misses for stable data.
+
+During peak traffic periods, the high cache miss rate for pricing queries has become a bottleneck, requiring additional database connections and increasing latency for downstream services that depend on this data. Analysis of historical pricing changes shows that data remains consistent for hours or even days between updates, making the current 15-minute window significantly more aggressive than necessary for business requirements.
+
+## Decision
+
+We have decided to increase the pricing cache TTL from 900 seconds to 3600 seconds (1 hour). This change aligns the cache duration with the actual frequency of pricing updates and reduces unnecessary backend pressure. The one-hour window provides sufficient freshness for business use cases while delivering meaningful reductions in cache misses and database load during normal operations.
+
+This adjustment does not require changes to the cache invalidation strategy; existing cache invalidation procedures triggered by explicit pricing updates will continue to clear stale entries immediately when needed, ensuring that intentional changes propagate quickly to consumers.
+
+## Consequences
+
+**Positive consequences:** Reducing the cache miss rate will decrease load on the pricing service backend by an estimated 15-20%, lowering database connection pressure and improving response latency for pricing queries. Downstream services will experience more consistent performance during peak traffic periods, and overall infrastructure costs associated with pricing queries should decrease.
+
+**Trade-offs:** The one-hour TTL means that in edge cases where pricing data is updated outside of the standard invalidation procedure, consumers may see stale prices for up to one hour. This is acceptable given the rarity of unannounced pricing changes and the existence of explicit invalidation paths for standard updates. Teams working with pricing data should be aware of this window when troubleshooting discrepancies between the cache and the authoritative pricing database.
